summary:
The Falkland Islands are a British Overseas Territory with its own Legislative Assembly, which makes law for the territory. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1989, and the age of consent has been equal since 2005.

Same-sex marriage and civil partnerships have been available since 29 April 2017. The Legislative Assembly passed the bill in March 2017 by 7 votes to 1, and the registrar general confirmed by reply in June 2017 that it is law. Civil partnerships are open to opposite-sex couples as well as same-sex couples.

The Constitution Order 2008, at Article 16, bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The sources identify sexual orientation only; no gender-identity ground is stated in the Constitution.

United Kingdom frameworks do not reach the Islands. The UK Equality Act 2010 and the Gender Recognition Act 2004 do not extend to the Falkland Islands, so protection and recognition depend on the territory's own ordinances.

Legal gender change has been possible since 2014. There is no self-identification route and no recognition of non-binary status, and holders of a UK Gender Recognition Certificate are recognised in their acquired gender under the CPE Ordinance 2014.

Three ordinances frame the criminal-justice treatment of bias. The Crimes Ordinance 2014 provides for hate-stirring on grounds of sexual orientation, the CPE Ordinance 2014 provides for sexual orientation as an aggravating factor in sentencing, and a Prisons Ordinance was enacted in 2017.
tangentialFactors:
Public consultation ahead of the 2017 reform recorded 90% support for same-sex marriage and 94% for civil partnerships in a territory of roughly 3,000 residents, and the sources characterise local attitudes as largely positive.

The United Kingdom is responsible for the defence of the Falkland Islands, while day-to-day legislation is made locally; a visitor's exposure to rights protection therefore turns on local ordinances rather than on UK statutes.

The dependency of South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands sits outside this regime: the registrar general confirmed in June 2017 that same-sex marriage is not legal there, so travel between the two carries a different legal position.
localsOnly:
Stepchild adoption and joint adoption have been available to same-sex couples since 2017.

Residents seeking to change their legal gender must use the court-based process introduced in 2014; there is no declaration-based self-identification, and no non-binary marker is available on local documents.

Civil partnerships are available to opposite-sex residents as well as to same-sex couples, giving local couples a second legal form alongside marriage.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not identify a gender-identity ground in the Constitution Order 2008; whether any local statute or ordinance supplies equivalent protection on that ground is unresolved in this inventory.

No sourced enforcement data exists here for the Crimes Ordinance 2014 hate-stirring provision or the CPE Ordinance 2014 aggravating-factor provision: no prosecutions, sentences or reported incidents are documented in the inventory.

The Prisons Ordinance 2017 is cited by name only; its treatment of trans detainees, including placement and healthcare, is not specified in the sources.

Nothing in the inventory addresses trans-specific healthcare access, gender-marker treatment at ports of entry, or facilities access on the Islands.

For South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands, only the absence of same-sex marriage is sourced; the remainder of that dependency's legal position for trans visitors is unresolved.
